questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: In the early fasting state, blood glucose is maintained principally by:
questions.concept: Liver glycogen stores last about 18 to 24 hours, after which gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids predominates. Muscle glycogen cannot contribute as muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Ketone bodies are synthesised in the:
options: Liver mitochondria, but the liver cannot use them due to lack of thiophorase
questions.concept: Absence of succinyl-CoA acetoacetyl-CoA transferase in liver ensures ketones are exported for use by brain, heart and muscle, an elegant example of metabolic division of labour.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: The predominant ketone body in diabetic ketoacidosis is:
questions.concept: Standard urine nitroprusside dipsticks detect acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, so ketonuria may underestimate severity and can paradoxically appear to worsen during treatment as the ratio shifts.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: The brain adapts to prolonged starvation by:
options: Using ketone bodies for up to two-thirds of its energy needs
questions.concept: This adaptation spares muscle protein by reducing the gluconeogenic demand, which is the principal determinant of survival time in starvation. Fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Insulin promotes all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue
questions.concept: Insulin is the master anabolic hormone and actively inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase. Its deficiency releases this brake, driving the lipolysis and ketogenesis of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: The Cori cycle involves:
options: Transport of muscle lactate to the liver for conversion back to glucose
questions.concept: It shifts the metabolic burden of anaerobic glycolysis to the liver at a net ATP cost. The glucose-alanine cycle similarly carries nitrogen from muscle to liver for urea synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: HbA1c reflects glycaemic control over approximately:
questions.concept: Non-enzymatic glycation is proportional to average glucose over the red cell lifespan. It is falsely low in haemolysis and blood loss and falsely high in iron deficiency, limiting reliability in those settings.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Metabolic syndrome centres on insulin resistance, which biochemically causes:
options: Raised triglycerides with low HDL and small dense LDL particles
questions.concept: Failure to suppress lipolysis floods the liver with free fatty acids, driving VLDL overproduction. LDL cholesterol is not itself a diagnostic criterion of the syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: Alcohol causes hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis because its metabolism:
options: Raises the NADH to NAD+ ratio, blocking gluconeogenesis
questions.concept: Excess NADH drives pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, removing both gluconeogenic substrates. This also promotes fatty liver by favouring triglyceride synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Integration of metabolism: fed/fasting, diabetes, ketosis
questions.stem: In the fed state, the principal fate of excess dietary glucose is:
options: Glycogen synthesis followed by conversion to fatty acids for storage as triglyceride
questions.concept: Insulin activates glycogen synthase and lipogenesis while inhibiting the opposing pathways, ensuring reciprocal regulation so that synthesis and breakdown never run simultaneously as a futile cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation relates blood pH to:
options: The ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid (dissolved CO2)
questions.concept: pH depends on the ratio, not absolute values, which is why compensation restores pH by adjusting the other component. Normal ratio is 20 to 1, giving pH 7.4.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The anion gap is calculated as:
options: Sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate, normally 8 to 12 mmol/L
questions.concept: It represents unmeasured anions, principally albumin, so it must be corrected in hypoalbuminaemia by adding 2.5 for every 1 g/dL fall. A raised gap indicates added acid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The most important extracellular buffer system is:
options: The bicarbonate-carbonic acid system, because it is open to respiratory adjustment
questions.concept: Although its pKa of 6.1 is not ideal, the ability to vary carbon dioxide by ventilation and bicarbonate by the kidney makes it uniquely powerful. Haemoglobin is the main intracellular buffer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Iron is absorbed principally in the:
options: Duodenum, enhanced by vitamin C and the ferrous form
questions.concept: Hepcidin from the liver is the master regulator, blocking ferroportin-mediated release. Its induction by inflammation explains the anaemia of chronic disease with low iron but raised ferritin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Copper deficiency causes anaemia because copper is required for:
options: Ceruloplasmin (ferroxidase) activity, needed to mobilise iron
questions.concept: Copper deficiency causes a microcytic anaemia unresponsive to iron, with neutropenia and neurological features. Menkes kinky hair disease results from defective copper absorption and transport.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Iodine deficiency in the fetus causes:
options: Cretinism with intellectual disability and deaf-mutism
questions.concept: Universal salt iodisation is the principal preventive strategy, and iodine deficiency remains the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide. Goitre reflects TSH-driven thyroid hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Fluoride in drinking water at optimal levels prevents dental caries, but excess causes:
questions.concept: The optimal level is about 0.5 to 0.8 mg/L in India. Mottled enamel appears above 1.5 mg/L and crippling skeletal fluorosis with genu valgum above 3 mg/L, a serious problem in several Indian states.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Magnesium deficiency should be suspected in refractory:
options: Hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia that do not correct until magnesium is replaced
questions.concept: Magnesium is required for PTH secretion and action and for renal potassium conservation, so correcting it is a prerequisite for correcting the other electrolytes - a common clinical trap.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: In metabolic acidosis, respiratory compensation is predicted by the Winter formula:
options: Expected PCO2 equals 1.5 times bicarbonate plus 8, plus or minus 2
questions.concept: If measured PCO2 exceeds the predicted value there is an additional respiratory acidosis, and if lower an additional respiratory alkalosis - allowing detection of mixed disorders.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes, and its deficiency causes:
options: Poor wound healing, impaired taste, diarrhoea and acral dermatitis
questions.concept: Zinc supplementation shortens childhood diarrhoea and reduces recurrence, which is why the national programme pairs zinc with ORS. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is the inherited absorptive defect.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: An oncogene differs from a proto-oncogene in that it is:
options: An activated, gain-of-function form driving unregulated proliferation
questions.concept: A single activated allele suffices, making oncogenes dominant at the cellular level, whereas tumour suppressors require loss of both alleles - the Knudson two-hit hypothesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The RAS oncogene causes malignant transformation because the mutant protein:
options: Remains locked in the GTP-bound active state due to loss of GTPase activity
questions.concept: RAS mutations occur in about 30% of human cancers, notably pancreatic, colorectal and lung. KRAS status predicts resistance to anti-EGFR antibodies in colorectal cancer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Telomerase is significant in cancer because it:
options: Maintains telomere length, allowing unlimited replicative capacity
questions.concept: Normal somatic cells lose telomere length each division until replicative senescence. Most cancers reactivate telomerase, achieving immortality - one of the recognised hallmarks of cancer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Alpha-fetoprotein is a useful tumour marker for:
options: Hepatocellular carcinoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours
questions.concept: CEA is used for colorectal, PSA for prostate, CA-125 for ovarian and CA 19-9 for pancreatic cancer. Markers are best for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence, not for screening.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The BCL2 gene contributes to malignancy by:
options: Inhibiting apoptosis, allowing survival of cells that should die
questions.concept: The t(14;18) translocation in follicular lymphoma places BCL2 under immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter control, causing overexpression - a tumour arising from failure of cell death rather than excess proliferation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Angiogenesis in tumours is driven principally by:
questions.concept: Tumours cannot grow beyond 1 to 2 mm without a blood supply. Bevacizumab targets VEGF, and anti-VEGF agents are also used intravitreally for wet age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The Warburg effect describes tumour reliance on:
questions.concept: This shift provides biosynthetic intermediates for rapid growth and underlies FDG-PET imaging, which localises tumours by their avid glucose uptake.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The p53 protein is described as the guardian of the genome because it:
options: Arrests the cell cycle at G1/S for repair or triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable
questions.concept: Loss of p53 permits damaged cells to proliferate. Germline mutation causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome with multiple early cancers, and HPV E6 protein degrades p53 in cervical carcinogenesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes function in:
options: Homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks
questions.concept: Their loss creates dependence on alternative repair, exploited therapeutically by PARP inhibitors through synthetic lethality. Carriers face high breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer risk.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Cancer cachexia is mediated principally by:
options: Cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6 causing hypermetabolism and proteolysis
questions.concept: Because it is cytokine-driven rather than simple starvation, cachexia is not reversed by feeding alone. It predicts poor prognosis and reduced tolerance of chemotherapy.
